topic.title: The vitamin became a dessert
topic.claim: Wellness brands turned vitamins into gummies because you'll take a sweet every day and forget a pill.
topic.moment: A jar of 'sleep gummies' next to the laptop, two eaten at once because they taste nice.

turn.believed: Gummies are a better, gentler way to take supplements.
turn.actually: They're a habit product dressed as health, often with less of the active thing and some sugar.

topic.because: A brand needs you to come back every month. Candy you enjoy gets reordered; a pill you dread doesn't.
topic.payoff: Read the label once. If sugar is near the top, you're buying a sweet with a promise.
topic.behaviour: People buy biotin, ashwagandha and melatonin gummies on subscription and eat them like snacks.
topic.mechanism: Taste drives repeat orders, and repeat orders are the business.
topic.send_to: The colleague with four gummy jars on their desk.
topic.why_now: Gummy supplements are now on every quick-commerce home screen.

score.why: Wellness is marketing wearing a yoga mat; gummies are a habit product, which most people never think about.

The take's premise is wrong: Premise 4, that gummies often hold less of the active ingredient, fails for the product the post builds its story around. It is true of multivitamin and magnesium gummies. But the reader is eating sleep gummies, and the most-cited independent test of melatonin gummies (JAMA, 2023) found that most of them hold more than the label says, not less. So the punchline 'that second one wasn't a dose, it was dessert' is backwards. Two melatonin gummies can mean a double or even several-times dose. Premise 1 is also overstated. Brands moved to gummies because people asked for them: they're tired of pills, can't swallow them, or like the taste. One-tap reorder and subscriptions are sold for tablets just as much, so reordering isn't something only gummies get. Premise 5 is half right. Gummies have a limited amount of room for active ingredient, and bulky nutrients like calcium, magnesium and iron are hard to fit, so they are often cut. The sweet base is simply what a gummy is made of. It isn't 'filling a gap'. The claim that sugar is why you take a second one is the post's guess, not a finding.. How it actually works: Gummy supplements grew because buyers wanted an easier, tastier format. Brands meet that demand with a sugar-and-gelatin or pectin base, which only leaves room for a limited amount of active ingredient. That's why gummy multivitamins usually carry fewer nutrients and lower doses than tablets yet cost more per day (Which? found 15p vs 7p a day for Boots' versions). For sleep gummies the risk runs the other way. The label is often inaccurate: one test found 74% to 347% of the stated melatonin, so an extra gummy is an uncontrolled extra dose, not just a sweet. Rebuild the post on the correct mechanism.
Could not verify: 'Wellness/vitamin brands' apps send reorder prompts such as 'Running low? Reorder in one tap' with one-tap reordering.'. Cut it, or state it only if a source says it.

c2.correct: I found no first-party page or announcement showing that a wellness or vitamin brand's app sends the prompt 'Running low? Reorder in one tap'. What exists is Shopify merchant tools (Reorder Reminder Pro, Easy Reorder) that send email reminders with a one-click reorder link. Care/of's app lets users manage upcoming orders. None of these matches the quoted wording or an in-app push with one-tap reorder. Brand-specific wording should be dropped or confirmed in the app itself.

sources.quote: sends a reminder email with a one-click reorder link
sending a reminder before a customer runs out and linking to a one-click reorder page

c5.correct: Which? testing found that gummies often provide lower doses than tablets, for example magnesium at 150mg for a Holland & Barrett gummy versus 300mg for its tablet. This is product-testing evidence, not a universal rule, so 'often' is the right wording.

sources.quote: they often contain lower doses of nutrients than traditional supplements.
gummy multivitamins selected for testing contained only 14% of their listed vitamin D in several cases

c7.correct: FDA requires ingredients to be listed in descending order of predominance by weight, so sugar near the top means it is a major component. This applies to the 'Other ingredients' list. Ingredients already declared in the Supplement Facts panel don't need repeating there.

sources.quote: You must list the ingredients in descending order of predominance by weight.

sources.publisher: U.S. Code of Federal Regulations, 21 CFR 101.4
sources.quote: ingredients ... shall be listed ... in descending order of predominance by weight

c8.correct: Gummies are generally priced above tablets and above sweets. Which? found per-dose gummy prices up to 8x the tablet price, for example Boots gummies at 15p per dose against 7p for the tablets.

sources.quote: Boots Multivitamin gummies: 15p per dose. Boots A-Z Multivitamin tablets: 7p per dose.
Centrum gummies cost 29 cents per recommended dose of two gummies, more than three times the cost of the pill form.

c9.correct: Taking more than the labelled serving exceeds the labelled dose. In multivitamins, extra gummies can push several nutrients over the intended amount. The claim's wording 'not a proper dose' is a reasonable paraphrase. Risk depends on the ingredients, mainly fat-soluble vitamins, iron and calcium.

sources.quote: if you take more than the serving size (usually one vitamin), you can overdose on all the vitamins that make up your multivitamin.
Fat-soluble vitamins (like A, D, E, and K) don't get flushed out in the urine, so they're the most likely to cause vitamin toxicity.

c11.correct: Gen Z and Millennials favour gummies. ADM 2024 data show 38% of Gen Z and 30% of Millennials prefer gummies over traditional formats. A 2022 Unwinder survey of Gen Z found half take a gummy multivitamin. Gummies are about 35% of supplement format use across all US adults. 'Popular' holds, but 'the most common format' would not, because capsules and tablets still lead.

sources.quote: Millennials and Gen Z are at the forefront of this gummy revolution, with 30% and 38%, respectively, favoring gummies over traditional formats.
half of those surveyed take a multivitamin in the form of a gummy, compared with 35% who take a pill

News coverage of the JAMA research letter (doi:10.1001/jama.2023.2296), which tested 25 melatonin gummy products: 22 of the 25 were mislabeled, and the melatonin in them ranged from 74% to 347% of the labeled amount. I couldn't open the JAMA letter itself, so this wording is the coverage's summary, not a direct quote from the paper.

_ledger.text:
[cover] Your vitamins became [gummies] because a sweet gets reordered
The taste is what keeps you buying the jar.
 

[slide 1] Your vitamins became gummies because a sweet gets reordered.
Swipe to read →

[slide 2] It's past midnight and the laptop is still open. The jar of sleep gummies sits next to it, lid half on.
The label says one. You eat two because they taste like the mango candy from school, then lick the sugar dust off your fingers.

[slide 3] A few weeks later the app pings: "Running low? Reorder in one tap." You tap, and add the biotin ones for your hair.
The multivitamin strip from the chemist is still in your drawer, three tablets popped, the rest expired. This feels like progress. You finally take something every day.

[slide 4] The brand couldn't care less if you slept better. It cares that the jar is empty by the 28th.
Your sleep never shows up on their sales sheet. That one-tap reorder does, every month, for as long as you like the taste.
The thing they're really selling is your next order.

[slide 5] Fair enough, if tablets make you gag, a gummy you eat beats a strip that expires in a drawer.
But the sweetness takes up room. Gummies often carry less of the active thing than a tablet, and sugar fills the gap. That's also why you reach for a second one.

[slide 6] Read the label once. If sugar is near the top, you're paying supplement prices for a sweet with a promise.
That second one you ate last night wasn't a dose. It was dessert.

[end card] Open this again before you tap reorder on that jar.
The colleague with four gummy jars on their desk.

[caption] The most consistent health habit this generation has is a sweet with a reorder button.

[alt text] A six-slide carousel arguing that wellness brands sell vitamins as gummies because a sweet people enjoy gets reordered every month. It follows a reader eating two sleep gummies next to their laptop at midnight, then reordering on an app while an expired tablet strip sits in a drawer. It says the brand earns from the empty jar, not the better sleep. It admits a gummy you take beats a pill you skip, but notes gummies often hold less of the active ingredient plus sugar. It ends with a test: if sugar is near the top of the label, the second gummy was dessert, not a dose.

notes: The take's premise is wrong: Premise 4, that gummies often hold less of the active ingredient, fails for the product the post builds its story around. It is true of multivitamin and magnesium gummies. But the reader is eating sleep gummies, and the most-cited independent test of melatonin gummies (JAMA, 2023) found that most of them hold more than the label says, not less. So the punchline 'that second one wasn't a dose, it was dessert' is backwards. Two melatonin gummies can mean a double or even several-times dose. Premise 1 is also overstated. One-tap reorder and subscriptions are sold for tablets just as much, so reordering isn't something only gummies get. Premise 5 is half right. Gummies have a limited amount of room for active ingredient, and bulky nutrients like calcium, magnesium and iron are hard to fit, so they are often cut. How it actually works: Gummy supplements grew because buyers wanted an easier, tastier format. Brands meet that demand with a sugar-and-gelatin or pectin base, which only leaves room for a limited amount of active ingredient. That's why gummy multivitamins usually carry fewer nutrients and lower doses than tablets yet cost more per day (Which? found 15p vs 7p a day for Boots' versions). For sleep gummies the risk runs the other way. The label is often inaccurate: one test found 74% to 347% of the stated melatonin, so an extra gummy is an uncontrolled extra dose, not just a sweet. Rebuild the post on the correct mechanism.

ledger.text: Gummy brands earn recurring monthly revenue from one-tap reorders for as long as the customer likes the taste.
ledger.sentence: That one-tap reorder does, every month, for as long as you like the taste.

ledger.text: Gummies often contain less of the active ingredient than equivalent tablets.
ledger.sentence: Gummies often carry less of the active thing than a tablet, and sugar fills the gap.

ledger.text: Gummy supplements contain sugar that takes up space in each piece, filling the room left by less active ingredient.
ledger.sentence: But the sweetness takes up room. ... and sugar fills the gap.

ledger.sentence: you're paying supplement prices for a sweet with a promise.

ledger.text: Taking two gummies when the label says one exceeds the labelled dose, so the extra is not a proper dose.
ledger.sentence: The label says one. You eat two ... That second one you ate last night wasn't a dose.

ledger.text: Gummies are more likely to be taken consistently than tablets by people who dislike swallowing tablets, so a gummy taken beats a tablet skipped.

ledger.text: Gummy vitamins are a popular, widely consumed habit among the current generation.
ledger.sentence: The most consistent health habit this generation has is a sweet with a reorder button.

c2.correct: I found no first-party page or announcement showing that a wellness or vitamin brand's app sends the prompt 'Running low? Reorder in one tap'. What exists is Shopify merchant tools (Reorder Reminder Pro, Easy Reorder) that send email reminders with a one-click reorder link. Care/of's app lets users manage upcoming orders. None of these matches the quoted wording or an in-app push with one-tap reorder. Brand-specific wording should be dropped or confirmed in the app itself.

sources.quote: sends a reminder email with a one-click reorder link
sending a reminder before a customer runs out and linking to a one-click reorder page

c5.correct: Which? testing found that gummies often provide lower doses than tablets, for example magnesium at 150mg for a Holland & Barrett gummy versus 300mg for its tablet. This is product-testing evidence, not a universal rule, so 'often' is the right wording.

sources.quote: they often contain lower doses of nutrients than traditional supplements.
gummy multivitamins selected for testing contained only 14% of their listed vitamin D in several cases

c7.correct: FDA requires ingredients to be listed in descending order of predominance by weight, so sugar near the top means it is a major component. This applies to the 'Other ingredients' list. Ingredients already declared in the Supplement Facts panel don't need repeating there.

sources.quote: You must list the ingredients in descending order of predominance by weight.

sources.publisher: U.S. Code of Federal Regulations, 21 CFR 101.4
sources.quote: ingredients ... shall be listed ... in descending order of predominance by weight

c8.correct: Gummies are generally priced above tablets and above sweets. Which? found per-dose gummy prices up to 8x the tablet price, for example Boots gummies at 15p per dose against 7p for the tablets.

sources.quote: Boots Multivitamin gummies: 15p per dose. Boots A-Z Multivitamin tablets: 7p per dose.
Centrum gummies cost 29 cents per recommended dose of two gummies, more than three times the cost of the pill form.

c9.correct: Taking more than the labelled serving exceeds the labelled dose. In multivitamins, extra gummies can push several nutrients over the intended amount. The claim's wording 'not a proper dose' is a reasonable paraphrase. Risk depends on the ingredients, mainly fat-soluble vitamins, iron and calcium.

sources.quote: if you take more than the serving size (usually one vitamin), you can overdose on all the vitamins that make up your multivitamin.
Fat-soluble vitamins (like A, D, E, and K) don't get flushed out in the urine, so they're the most likely to cause vitamin toxicity.

c11.correct: Gen Z and Millennials favour gummies. ADM 2024 data show 38% of Gen Z and 30% of Millennials prefer gummies over traditional formats. A 2022 Unwinder survey of Gen Z found half take a gummy multivitamin. Gummies are about 35% of supplement format use across all US adults. 'Popular' holds, but 'the most common format' would not, because capsules and tablets still lead.

sources.quote: Millennials and Gen Z are at the forefront of this gummy revolution, with 30% and 38%, respectively, favoring gummies over traditional formats.
half of those surveyed take a multivitamin in the form of a gummy, compared with 35% who take a pill

cover.headline: Your vitamins became [candy], so you eat them like candy
cover.sub: The taste fixed one problem and quietly made another.

paragraphs: Your vitamins became candy, so you eat them like candy.
slides.why_swipe: What's wrong with a vitamin you actually enjoy?

paragraphs: It's past midnight and the laptop is still open. The jar of sleep gummies sits next to it, lid half on.
The label says one. You eat two because they taste like the mango candy from the school canteen, then lick the sugar dust off your thumb.
slides.why_swipe: Isn't this still better than skipping pills?

paragraphs: To be fair, you asked for this. The multivitamin strip from the chemist is still in your drawer, three tablets popped, the rest expired.
Gummies fixed that. For the first time in years, you take something every single day.
slides.why_swipe: So where does it go wrong?

paragraphs: But you'd never swallow a second tablet because the first one tasted nice.
With a sleep gummy, that second one isn't a snack. It's a second dose of something meant to put you to sleep, chewed like a toffee.
**The sweetness switched off the part of you that counts doses.**
slides.why_swipe: And what about the ones you take for your hair and bones?

paragraphs: And the sweet base takes up room. A gummy can only hold so much, so bulky stuff like calcium or iron often gets cut or shrunk.
You end up paying more per day for less inside. The brand doesn't mind. A jar you enjoy is a jar you reorder.
slides.why_swipe: So how do you tell what's actually in your jar?

paragraphs: Read the label once. If sugar sits near the top, you're buying a sweet with a promise.
**Then look at where the jar lives: next to the laptop, beside the chips, where the medicine box has never been.**

end.save: Open this again before you reorder that jar.
end.send: The colleague with four gummy jars on their desk.
end.promise: How brands are really sold to you.

draft.caption: The most regular health habit of your twenties is a toffee with a label on it.
draft.alt_text: A six-slide carousel about gummy supplements. It follows a reader at midnight with a jar of sleep gummies next to the laptop, eating two because they taste like school candy. It admits gummies solved a real problem, since the old tablet strip expired in a drawer. Then it argues the taste makes people treat a dose like a snack, so a second sleep gummy is a second dose. It notes a gummy has limited room, so bulky nutrients like calcium or iron are often cut, and you pay more per day for less. It ends with a test: if sugar is near the top of the label, you're buying a sweet with a promise, and the jar sits next to the chips, not the medicine box.
